chunks: For by Allah, it is seriousness (reality), not play, and truth, not falsehood,
and it is none other than death; its caller is made to be heard, and its dragsman is made to hasten,
so let not the multitude of people deceive you regarding yourself,
for you have seen those who were before you, who amassed wealth, feared poverty, and felt safe from its consequences—the longevity of desire and the apparent distance from death—
how death overtook them, turning them out of their homelands, and took them from their places of safety,
borne on the beams of the coffins, with people busy about them one after another, carrying them on their shoulders and supporting them with their hands.

key_terms.حَادِيهِ: Its dragsman / guide (metaphor for the one who leads death)
key_terms.دَاعِيهِ: Its caller (metaphor for the call of death)
key_terms.سَوَادُ النَّاسِ: The multitude / blackness of the people

ai.seo_question: What does Nahj al-Balagha say about the reality of death and how it affects those who feel safe in this world?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) emphasizes that death is the ultimate reality ('al-jidd') that interrupts worldly playfulness, warning against the illusion of security created by the multitude of people. He illustrates how death abruptly seizes those who accumulated wealth and felt safe, carrying them away from their homes in coffins, a vivid imagery of the transient nature of worldly power. This counsel underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on *zuhd* (asceticism) and constant readiness for the Hereafter, reminding believers that death comes unexpectedly regardless of one's status or accumulated wealth.
